lesson.title: Acceleration: The Derivative of Velocity
lesson.summary: Acceleration measures how fast velocity itself is changing, so a(t) = v'(t), which also makes it the second derivative of position, a(t) = s''(t).
lesson.body:
Velocity can change from moment to moment: an object can speed up, slow down, or reverse direction. Acceleration is exactly the tool for measuring that change, instant by instant, the same way velocity measures how position is changing. Since velocity was just defined as the derivative of position, and acceleration is the derivative of velocity, acceleration ends up being the second derivative of position, tying directly back to the second-derivative concept from earlier in this unit.

Formally, a(t) = v'(t), and because v(t) = s'(t), this also means a(t) = s''(t). Both expressions describe the same function; you can compute acceleration either by differentiating velocity once or by differentiating position twice.

Continue with the position function from the previous chapter, s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t (meters, t in seconds), which gave velocity v(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9. Differentiate once more: a(t) = v'(t) = 6t - 12, which factors as a(t) = 6(t - 2). Evaluate at the same time values used before: a(0) = -12 m/s^2, a(1) = -6 m/s^2, a(2) = 0 m/s^2, a(3) = 6 m/s^2, and a(4) = 12 m/s^2. Notice acceleration here is not constant, it changes steadily with t, which is typical for real motion that isn't free fall or another constant-force situation.

Acceleration's units are always distance over time squared, m/s^2 in this example. It's worth noting that acceleration is not always changing like this; an object falling near Earth's surface under gravity alone has essentially constant acceleration, about 9.8 m/s^2 downward, which is a special case rather than the general rule. In the cubic example above, acceleration itself is a function of time, which sets up the next chapter: since a(t) is changing, it too can be differentiated.
